newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel defies calls to resign over tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Waigel defies calls to resign over tax reform.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Monday defied calls to resign from the wings of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's own Christian Democrat party (CDU) over major tax reforms he is due to finalise this week.
Waigel rejected as "improper and underhand" a salvo of demands for him to quit made up-and-coming CDU officials unhappy with coalition talk of raising value-added tax to finance income tax cuts.

But he quickly retreated from a coalition pact to raise VAT by two percentage points, saying a one-point hike in the 15 percent VAT rate would pay for income tax cuts without hurting ordinary Germans.
"That is a justifiable shift from direct to indirect taxation," Waigel said after a Munich meeting of his Christian Social Union (CSU), Bavarian sister party to Kohl's CDU.
After months of debate, a coalition tax working group is due on Thursday to finalise a tax shakeup to take effect in 1999 which will bring tax cuts of around 25 billion marks ($15 billion).

But, critics say, what started as a mission to simplify Germany's complex tax system has degenerated into a woolly debate. An opinion poll last week showed that a majority of Germans believed the reform's main aim was to increase VAT.
Christian Wulff, CDU party leader in Lower Saxony, led calls at the weekend for Waigel to step down, and kept up the pressure on Monday.
"If on Thursday the coalition does not decide on a big tax reform without increases in VAT and other taxes, then there should be a cabinet reshuffle," Wulff told SAT1 television.
Commenting on Waigel's change of position on Monday, Wulff said: "The CSU is slowly getting the idea that you can't cut (income) tax and put up VAT at the same time."
In what appeared to be a coordinated attack, other young Turks leading the CDU in Germany's provinces, joined the attack.

"The great challenge for government is to achieve a tax reform without hiking VAT," Peter Mueller, CDU head in Saarland province, told ARD public television. "If Theo Waigel cannot manage this, we must ask whether there are others who can."
Also among the critics were Hesse party chief Rudolf Koch and Hamburg's Ole von Beust -- all figures tipped to climb the CDU ladder once Kohl, 66, heads into retirement.

Waigel at the weekend received Kohl's full backing, and CDU general secretary Peter Hintze said the attacks were unfair and unjustified. "We will get a reform that deserves the name," Hintze told Berlin Radio on Monday.

But the criticism shows just how widespread dissatisfaction with Waigel's financial stewardship has become as Germany enters the year when it will find out whether it will make the grade for European monetary union.

Waigel badly missed borrowing targets last year, and faces a huge task to bring the budget deficit below the Maastricht treaty limit of three percent of gross domestic product. The deficit was 3.9 percent of GDP in 1996.

The constant airing of new tax proposals by the three coalition parties has also badly damaged consumer confidence, dampening economic recovery. The Bundesbank warned, too, that severe fiscal tightening could delay economic recovery.

With just three days left until a final coalition meeting on the tax plan, junior partners the Free Democrats (FDP) were still pushing a three-band income tax system with rates of 15, 25 and 35 percent. Waigel favours a sliding-scale system running from 19.5 percent to 39 percent. The top tax rate now is 50 percent.
The coalition's tax turmoil left the Social Democrats (SPD) opposition rubbing their hands with glee. Tax spokesman Joachim Poss said Waigel was a victim of promises he could not keep.
"Whoever wants to pay for income tax reforms by borrowing or raising VAT will fail at the outset, because the tax system will not become simpler or fairer," Poss told German radio.
